newsitem.title: USA: Clinton defends his welfare plan, raises money.
newsitem.headline: Clinton defends his welfare plan, raises money.

text.p: President Clinton ran into some criticism of his welfare proposals Tuesday on a visit to New York where he was also raising more than $1 million to help elect Democrats to the Senate.

At a roundtable discussion at the Riverside Church near Harlem on Manhattan's West Side, Clinton defended his efforts to get people off welfare rolls by offering tax credits and other incentives for businesses that hire welfare recipients.

Earl Graves, chief executive officer of Black Enterprise Magazine, reflected some frustration at Clinton's decision last summer to sign a Republican-backed welfare law that ended a 61-year federal entitlement to welfare. He said the law was "designed to destroy" the government's social safety net.

"It is unrealistic and unfair to expect the private sector in general and black-owned businesses in particular to sacrifice profit margins in order to do the government's job," Graves said. "Unlike the federal government, we can go out of business."

Clinton bristled at the criticism and heatedly defended his proposals in support of his second-term goal of getting jobs for one million welfare recipients in the next four years. He said government was still providing a safety net.
"Let me say, with all due respect, I don't think it's that simple," he said. "I don't think it's accurate to say that this bill destroys the safety net for poor people."

Nilda Roman, who has been on welfare for the last three years, complained of a lack of training for employment for poor people like herself and spoke of the demeaning way they are treated. "It's the way we're treated when we get there," she said. "I've seen the women clean the toilets. It's horrid and it's demeaning."

In later remarks at an awards lunch for the Business Enterprise Trust, Clinton said getting jobs for one million on welfare could be done if a commitment was made by the country's 826,000 businesses with more than 20 employees, 1.1 million non-profit organisations and 135,000 churches with more than 200 members to hire the underclass.
"Just look at the sheer numbers of employers out there -- we can do this million people in a snap and help to break the back of the isolated underclass of America," he said.

Clinton got a reminder of the other main purpose of his trip -- fund-raising -- on the motorcade drive to the church. An electronic billboard advertising Fairway supermarkets said, "Hey Mr. President ... Fairway coffee 35 cents a cup ... White House coffee $200,000 a cup and ours tastes so much better..."

At a time when Democratic fund-raising practices from last year's campaigns are under investigation, Clinton was going to the Upper East Side home of a wealthy donor, Shelby Bryan, to raise more than $1 million from 120 people at a reception.

In his remarks to them, he planned to encourage Democrats not to be scared away from contributing to the party at a time when it has been called into question. The fund-raiser came less than a month after he ballyhooed a new voluntary ban on gifts from foreign nationals and contributions over $100,000 at the Democratic National Committee.

Those rules did not apply to this event because it was sponsored by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and it has not adopted the new DNC regulations. The White House wants the Senate committee and its House counterpart to adopt the rules but does not feel it can dictate to them.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said there was a witch-hunt atmosphere in Washington that all fund-raisers were bad and urged reporters to be fair. "Unless the argument here is that we go to public financing and taxpayers pay for politics, there will be fund-raisers in the future. Candidates will have to raise money."

Republicans who outspent Democrats by far last year are busily replenishing their coffers as well. Some 200 Republican big spenders -- members of the party's exclusive "Team 100" -- were golfing, playing tennis and sunbathing with Republican officials and congressional leaders, including House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, at a posh Palm Beach, Fla., hotel resort this week.
